assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Galvanising
items.clue: Coating iron or steel with zinc.

items.label: Monomer
items.clue: The small molecule from which a polymer is built.

items.label: Alloy
items.clue: A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements.

items.label: Drying agent
items.clue: A substance such as anhydrous calcium chloride that removes water vapour, used to give a nail air without water.

questions.stem: Which method prevents corrosion by acting as a barrier?

options.text: Painting the surface so that air and water cannot reach the metal
Bolting blocks of magnesium along the outside of the pipe
Heating the metal strongly to harden its outside layer
Mixing carbon into the metal to turn it into an alloy

questions.explanation: Greasing, painting and electroplating are the barrier methods named by the specification; they keep air and water off the surface.

questions.stem: Duralumin is an alloy of aluminium with copper and magnesium. Its density is 2.8 g/cm3 and it is harder than pure aluminium. A titanium alloy has a density of 4.5 g/cm3 and is harder than duralumin. Which is the better choice for a lightweight bicycle frame that must not bend?

options.text: Titanium alloy, because it is the harder of the two
Duralumin, because it is far less dense and still hard
Titanium alloy, because a denser metal is always stronger
Pure aluminium, because it is stronger than any alloy

questions.stem: Aluminium is a reactive metal, yet aluminium window frames do not corrode away. Why not?

options.text: Aluminium is unreactive, so nothing in the air can attack it
An oxide coating forms that protects the metal underneath
Its oxide flakes away, leaving fresh clean metal behind
Frames are always painted before they are fitted

questions.explanation: Aluminium has an oxide coating that protects the metal from further corrosion.

questions.stem: Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy. Which metals is the gold usually mixed with?

options.text: The gold is mixed with silver, copper and zinc
Nothing else, since jewellery gold is pure
Iron and carbon, added to harden the gold
A compound of gold, silver, copper and zinc

questions.explanation: Gold used as jewellery is usually an alloy with silver, copper and zinc.

questions.stem: Blocks of metal are bolted to a steel ship's hull to give sacrificial protection. Which metal should be used?

options.text: Magnesium, as it is more reactive than iron and corrodes first
Copper, because it is less reactive and resists corrosion
Tin, because it sits below iron and will not be eaten away
Lead, because it is dense and very heavy for its size

questions.explanation: Sacrificial protection needs a metal above iron in the reactivity series, so it reacts in the iron's place.

questions.stem: What is high carbon steel used for?

options.text: Car body panels and sheeting
Cutlery and kitchen sinks
Cutting tools and sharp blades
Aeroplane bodies and frames

questions.explanation: High carbon steel is strong but brittle, which suits cutting tools and blades.

questions.stem: Iron sheets are galvanised. What does this mean?

options.text: They are coated with tin, a metal that resists corrosion
They are dipped in acid to clean them before painting
They are coated with zinc, which is more reactive
They are melted together with zinc as an alloy

questions.explanation: Galvanising is coating iron with zinc, a more reactive metal that gives sacrificial protection.

questions.stem: Aluminium alloys are used for the bodies of aircraft. Which property makes them suitable?

options.text: They are low density, so a given volume of them weighs less
They are the strongest metals known, so they never bend
They are dense, so they are tough enough for an aircraft.
They melt easily, so parts can be cast into shape

questions.explanation: Aluminium alloys are low density, so an aircraft body made from them is lighter to lift.

questions.stem: Which conditions are necessary for iron to rust?

options.text: Water alone; the air around the iron plays no part in it
Both air and water in contact with the iron surface
Air alone, since rust is simply an oxide of iron
Salt water only, as pure water cannot rust iron

questions.explanation: The specification states that both air and water are necessary for iron to rust.

questions.stem: Why are most metals in everyday use alloys rather than pure metals?

options.text: Alloys are compounds, so they cannot react with air at all
The mixture has properties, like hardness, that suit the job
Mixing metals always makes them much softer and easier to bend
Pure metals cost far too much to make in large amounts

questions.explanation: Most metals in everyday use are alloys because mixing gives more useful properties than the pure metal has.

questions.stem: A nail is sealed in a tube of air with anhydrous calcium chloride at the bottom. After a week it has not rusted. What does this show?

options.text: Calcium chloride is a chemical that prevents rust
Air plays no part in the rusting of iron at all
Sealing up the tube is what kept the nail shiny here
Dry air cannot rust iron, so water is needed

questions.explanation: The calcium chloride removes water vapour, so the nail has air but no water. It does not rust, so water is necessary as well.

questions.stem: Brass is used for musical instruments and door fittings. What is brass?

options.text: A mixture of copper and pure tin
A compound of copper and zinc
Iron with a thin copper coating
A mixture of copper and zinc

questions.explanation: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, which is why it is used for instruments and fittings.
